title: Chest Pain in the ED: Six Immediately Dangerous Diagnoses
subject: Emergency Triage
preview: Sudden chest pain with instability requires immediate assessment for acute coronary syndrome, aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism, tension pneumothorax, tamponade and esophageal rupture.
quickRevision: Sudden chest pain with instability requires immediate assessment for acute coronary syndrome, aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism, tension pneumothorax, tamponade and esophageal rupture.
Aortic dissection may feature abrupt maximal pain and pulse or blood pressure asymmetry; embolism may present with tachycardia, dyspnea and pleuritic pain.
Use pretest probability and focused examination to choose imaging; urgent threats take priority over labeling pain musculoskeletal.

sections.title: Recognize the situation
points: Sudden chest pain with instability requires immediate assessment for acute coronary syndrome, aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism, tension pneumothorax, tamponade and esophageal rupture.
History, vital signs and a 12-lead ECG guide early triage, but a single normal ECG cannot exclude acute coronary syndrome.

sections.title: Memory aid
points: For unstable chest pain, systematically consider six threats: acute coronary syndrome, aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism, tension pneumothorax, tamponade and esophageal rupture.
This is a red-flag checklist, not a diagnosis from symptoms alone.

sections.title: Exam trap — avoid this mistake
points: Do not discharge a high-risk patient solely because the first troponin or ECG is normal.
